findings.detail: The safety policy has two incompatible authorities and no common seam. policy.js carries a `legacy` leaf schema (controls: sanitation/drift/secrets/git_ci; enforcement: shell/web/mcp) and a `current` one (controls: sanitation.harness/drift.exact_copy/drift.semantic/secrets.deterministic/network.action_policy; enforcement: host.shell/host.web/host.mcp/git.pre_commit/ci.repo). The shipped default policy is the legacy document: no section switches, no `network` object, and therefore none of the four protected categories (outbound_network, remote_content_execution, sensitive_environment_read, guardrail_bypass) that business-spec §2 and §8.2 make the core of default-deny. effectiveStatus understands both shapes; evaluateAction understands only the legacy keys and ignores policy.enabled and policy.enforcement.enabled outright. Consequences: a user who disables enforcement globally is told 'unprotected' by status while the evaluator still returns `deny` (AT-BASE-5 inverted); a user on the documented authoritative schema who disables `host.shell` is ignored by the evaluator because it looks up `enforcement['shell']`; and drift.exact_copy cannot be disabled independently of drift.semantic (AT-B1). Gate 2 §8.6 requires one evaluator as the single seam, and this is two engines with disjoint key spaces.

No mechanical enforcement surface exists on any host, so the default-deny promise has no mechanism behind it. evaluateAction has exactly one production caller in the whole tree: networkPolicyDecision, which fires only for http-transport MCP config, hardcodes `category: 'network_access'` (not one of the four NETWORK_CATEGORIES), and whose own comment states the decision 'does not block config emission ... the runtime hook that fires when the entry is used is' — and that hook does not exist. The AT-HOST-1 test asserts at line 545 that no shell_hook, web_hook, or mcp_hook axis may be `emitted` on any of the 19 hosts. So AT-HOST-2's 'mechanically denied' and AT-BASE-2's shell and web coverage are satisfied by a pure function with no call site, and the per-axis `not_integrated` gap record is the only honest artifact in the area.

Enforcement reads the wrong file and fails open. activeNetworkPolicy() loads `.rig/network-policy.json` — the user-owned *candidate* — rather than the `.rig/policy/active.json` bundle, so editing the candidate changes the decision immediately with no approval, no digest, and no activation. That is exactly what AT-BASE-4 forbids ('when the user has not approved the exact new policy digest, then active permissions do not change') and what §8.3 forbids ('Enforcement reads only a fully valid active bundle'). The `catch { return baselineNetworkPolicy(); }` on line 210-212 also silently substitutes defaults for a malformed policy, contradicting §3's explicit carry-over constraint that the new path must fail closed on malformed user content rather than treating it as empty, and §10's 'fail closed on missing/stale/replay' row.

Roughly half the catalogue is machine-interpolated template text. `product-security/license-compliance/attribution/slices/floor.md:5` reads 'Policy grade slice. This slice bounds attribution to license-compliance.attribution. It uses `attribution-slice-floor` and checks notice_paths (nonempty): notice paths must name the concrete repository contract.' and `development/code-creation/refactoring/slices/floor.md:5` is the same sentence with only the service id, check id, and field name substituted. The four license-compliance minimal.md files share two whole paragraphs varying only by interpolation plus one synonym swap ('Tie acceptance to' / 'Ground the decision in'). AT-SHAPE-6 states that 'TODOs, interpolation artifacts, repeated filler, and merely non-empty fragments fail', and the D23 note recorded that hand-varied filler at scale 'only reproduces the 432-file placeholder-gaming problem the gate exists to catch'. The mechanical gate cannot see it: catalog.js:310-313 hashes whole normalized bodies, so interpolating the service name makes every body unique. The case anticipates this — 'mechanical presence checks alone do not pass' — and the project's own 2026-10-20 trace independently records 'repeated cue blocks ... a mechanical scan alone cannot be reported as semantic signoff'. Note the individual fragments are honest about their evidence limit ('The rule proves only that a value was configured'), which the amended case asks for; the defect is the repetition, not dishonesty.

The only mutating lint-format action has the weakest trust boundary in the leaf. Line 791 is `if (!approval || !approval.verified) throw` — a caller-supplied boolean object authorizes an arbitrary command, with no digest, no signature, and no binding to cmd.argv, while AT-LF-14 and AT-LF-20 in the same module consume real SSHSIG receipts bound to the plan digest. The test passes `{ verified: true }`, which is precisely the 'bare digest flag is never approval' shape §6.1 rules out. Separately, `if (cmd.verify)` on line 808 makes re-verification optional: omit `verify` and autofix mutates the tree and returns `verification: 'skipped'`, so AT-LF-12's required 're-verifies by re-running the check' can be skipped. Gate 2 §9.4 concedes the argv binding as 'an acknowledged hardening gap outside the frozen AT-LF-12 contract', but the frozen case says 'the user explicitly invokes a specific fix command under its own approval' — an approval not bound to the command cannot establish that the user approved that command.

findings.anchor: wiki/gate1/business-spec.md D24 revision note vs wiki/gate1/gate1.sig
findings.detail: The re-signed oracle contains a revision note whose own heading is 'Revision note (owner ratification pending) — D24 release and catalogue alignment', while gate1.sig has been re-signed over exactly those bytes in this worktree. Under business-spec §8 and AT-GATE-2 the signature *is* the ratification, so the frozen text asserts that the freeze covering it has not happened. A reader cannot resolve which statement governs, and the gate contract ('After signature, only the key holder may amend and re-sign the oracle') gives the signature precedence over a note claiming otherwise. The note should carry its ratification date and decision id, or the oracle should not be signed over it.

findings.anchor: AT-HOST-1 amendment (wiki/gate1/acceptance.md) vs business-spec §2 'Rig builds and emits for every host, through one uniform path' and §3 in-scope
findings.detail: This round rewrote AT-HOST-1 from 'complete per-axis contract' for 'any host live-hook axis Rig emits' to a three-state 'honest per-axis contract' admitting `not_integrated`. Business intent was not amended alongside it: §2 still requires that Rig 'emits for every host, through one uniform path', that 'no code path skips a host', and that emitting nothing is 'permitted only for an evidence-backed genuinely unsupported axis'; §3 still scopes in 'built adapters and emitted configuration for all 19 hosts'. With zero live-hook axes emitted anywhere and 11 of 19 hosts carrying no instruction artifact (AT-P4's own table), `not_integrated` is now absorbing cases §2 reserves for evidence-backed vendor absence. The honesty improvement is real and welcome; the problem is that acceptance moved and the business rule it implements did not, so the two documents now describe different products.

The whole baseline-and-user-control section is 3-to-9-line pure-function assertions against a fixture that is not the product's policy document. policyFixture emits `controls: {sanitation, drift, secrets, git_ci}`, `enforcement: {shell, web, mcp}`, and a top-level `allow: []` — none of §8.2's dotted leaf IDs, no section switches, no `network` object, no `network.default`, no categories. AT-BASE-7 (line 271-275) only asserts that validatePolicy throws on an added key and never asserts that the fixture itself validates, so it would pass unchanged if validatePolicy rejected every document — a tautological green. AT-BASE-5 (line 255-261) calls effectiveStatus, a label function, and never attempts a formerly restricted action, which is the behavior the case names. AT-HOST-2 (line 571) uses `category: 'credential_read'`, not NETWORK_CATEGORIES' `sensitive_environment_read`, so the four protected categories are never exercised anywhere in the oracle and the test asserts the echo of an invalid category as the matched 'rule'. These tests cannot fail for the reasons their cases describe.

Three frozen cases are certified by harnesses that do not execute the shipping behavior. AT-INSTALL-1 feeds resumeInstall a synthetic `operations` array with `interrupt_after: 2` rather than interrupting the real apply at a write boundary, and never asserts that `policy status`, the install line, or a run report withhold the protection claim — the exact failure D14 exists to prevent. AT-REPORT-1 asserts only that projectCiResult drops a `detail` field; the gitignore exclusion, the absence of a reports/rig/ artifact-upload step across all six providers, and the seeded-string grep of a captured failing job log are all absent, so the disclosure boundary itself is untested. AT-GATE-3 validates a hand-built receipt and asserts exactly one rejection (same-session); stale digests, an incomplete verdict set, and non-empty `unresolved` are not asserted as rejections, and the receipt shape carries no implementation-worktree digest or PR base, so AD-36 — the binding under which this review is issued — has no executable contract.

The amended case now names an internal implementation API inside the frozen oracle: 'a Context review created from `createGradeReviewRequest({ target, changed, commands })`'. The AT-LF-7 and AT-LF-9 rewrites are genuine strengthenings — AT-LF-7 now forbids the caller-supplied `result: { exit_code: 0 }` objects the removed tests relied on — but pinning a function signature in Gate 1 inverts the stated direction of authority ('the code adapts to the signed oracle') and means an ordinary refactor of a private helper requires a new owner signing ceremony. State the observable requirement and let the traceability row name the entry point.

Two install-manifest shapes coexist. AT-UNINSTALL-2 drives the designed append-only journal through the real journalWriter and readManifest, while AT-UNINSTALL-1 hand-writes a `.rig/install-manifest.json` object with a `records` array — a different filename and shape from §7.6's `.rig/install-manifest.jsonl`. Whichever is vestigial should be removed; §7.6's whole argument rests on one journal being the single removal authority, and a second accepted shape is a second authority.

The identical assertion `assert.doesNotMatch(text, /TODO|TBD|Concrete convention/i, file)` appears twice, at lines 209 and 211, with the distinct interpolation/filler assertion between them. Harmless but it reads as a merge artifact in a signed, manifested test file, where every byte requires an owner re-signature to correct.
